## Warm-up: meet the data

A small made-up dataset of 50 workers: hourly wage, years of education and years of experience. Run the cell to look at it.

```{webr}
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
educ  <- round(runif(n, 8, 20))
exper <- round(runif(n, 0, 30))
wage  <- exp(1 + 0.08 * educ + 0.02 * exper + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3))
d <- data.frame(wage, educ, exper)

head(d)
summary(lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper, data = d))
```

::: {.column-margin}
[we built the data with β_educ = 0.08, so we know the truth]{.scribble}
:::

Find the coefficient on `educ` in the output. It should be near 0.08: each extra year of education is associated with roughly 8% higher wages, holding experience fixed. Now let's rebuild that number from scratch.

## Exercise 1: OLS by the formula

The lesson gave you $\hat\beta = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y$. In R, `t(X)` is the transpose, `%*%` is matrix multiplication, and `solve(A)` is the inverse of `A`. The matrix `X` and vector `y` are already built for you.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ols_formula
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
educ  <- round(runif(n, 8, 20))
exper <- round(runif(n, 0, 30))
wage  <- exp(1 + 0.08 * educ + 0.02 * exper + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3))
d <- data.frame(wage, educ, exper)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ols_formula
X <- cbind(1, d$educ, d$exper)   # a column of 1s, then the regressors
y <- log(d$wage)

beta_hat <- ______
beta_hat
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ols_formula
#| check: true
target <- with(.envir_result, unname(coef(lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper, data = d))))
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 3 &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), target, tolerance = 1e-6))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Exactly what lm() gets. That one line is the heart of lm().")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not quite. You should get 3 numbers that match coef(lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper, data = d)).")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ols_formula"}
Read the formula from left to right: the inverse of `t(X) %*% X`, times `t(X)`, times `y`. Each piece needs `%*%` between it and the next.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ols_formula"}
```r
X <- cbind(1, d$educ, d$exper)
y <- log(d$wage)

beta_hat <- solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% y
beta_hat
```

In practice `solve(t(X) %*% X, t(X) %*% y)` is faster and numerically safer, because it avoids computing an inverse explicitly.
:::

## Exercise 2: the right angle

The lesson claimed residuals are always at a right angle to every regressor, so $X^\top \hat\varepsilon = 0$. Compute the residuals and check the claim.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: orthogonal
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
educ  <- round(runif(n, 8, 20))
exper <- round(runif(n, 0, 30))
wage  <- exp(1 + 0.08 * educ + 0.02 * exper + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3))
d <- data.frame(wage, educ, exper)
X <- cbind(1, d$educ, d$exper)
y <- log(d$wage)
beta_hat <- solve(t(X) %*% X) %*% t(X) %*% y
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: orthogonal
y_hat <- X %*% beta_hat      # fitted values
e     <- ______              # residuals: actual minus fitted

t(X) %*% e                   # should be (numerically) zero
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: orthogonal
#| check: true
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 3 && all(abs(.result) < 1e-8)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "All three are zero up to rounding error (numbers like 1e-13). The residuals are orthogonal to every column of X, including the column of 1s, which is why residuals always sum to zero when there's an intercept.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The result should be three numbers that are essentially zero. Check how you defined the residuals.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="orthogonal"}
A residual is the gap between what happened and what the line predicts: `y` minus `y_hat`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="orthogonal"}
```r
y_hat <- X %*% beta_hat
e     <- y - y_hat
t(X) %*% e
```
:::

## Exercise 3: R² by hand

$R^2 = 1 - \text{RSS}/\text{TSS}$. Compute it and compare with what `summary()` reports.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: rsq
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
educ  <- round(runif(n, 8, 20))
exper <- round(runif(n, 0, 30))
wage  <- exp(1 + 0.08 * educ + 0.02 * exper + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3))
d <- data.frame(wage, educ, exper)
fit <- lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper, data = d)
y <- log(d$wage)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: rsq
e   <- residuals(fit)
RSS <- sum(e^2)
TSS <- ______          # total variation of y around its mean

1 - RSS / TSS
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: rsq
#| check: true
target <- with(.envir_result, summary(fit)$r.squared)
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && abs(.result - target) < 1e-8) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("R² = %.3f, matching summary(fit). About %.0f%% of the variation in log wages is accounted for by education and experience.", target, 100 * target))
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not yet. TSS is the sum of squared deviations of y from its mean.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="rsq"}
`sum((y - mean(y))^2)`
:::

::: {.solution exercise="rsq"}
```r
e   <- residuals(fit)
RSS <- sum(e^2)
TSS <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
1 - RSS / TSS
```
:::

## Exercise 4: heteroskedasticity and robust standard errors

The slides' example is $y_i = 1 + 3x_i + x_i\,\varepsilon_i$: the bigger $|x_i|$, the noisier $y_i$. The usual standard-error formula assumes the noise is the same everywhere, so here it's wrong. Run the cell to see the fan shape.

```{webr}
set.seed(3)
x <- runif(200, -3, 3)
y <- 1 + 3 * x + x * rnorm(200)
plot(x, y, pch = 19, col = "#1B2559AA", main = "Noise grows with |x|")
abline(lm(y ~ x), col = "#2463EB", lwd = 3)
```

The **heteroskedasticity-robust** (HC0, or "sandwich") variance estimate replaces $\hat\sigma^2 (X^\top X)^{-1}$ with

$$
\hat V = (X^\top X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_i X_i X_i^\top \hat\varepsilon_i^2\Big)(X^\top X)^{-1}.
$$

The two slices of bread are the same $(X^\top X)^{-1}$; the filling lets each observation bring its own error size. Fill in the filling.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: sandwich
set.seed(3)
x <- runif(200, -3, 3)
y <- 1 + 3 * x + x * rnorm(200)
fit <- lm(y ~ x)
X <- cbind(1, x)
e <- residuals(fit)
bread <- solve(t(X) %*% X)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: sandwich
meat <- t(X) %*% diag(______) %*% X      # sum of X_i X_i' e_i^2
V_robust <- bread %*% meat %*% bread

c(classical = summary(fit)$coefficients["x", "Std. Error"],
  robust    = sqrt(V_robust[2, 2]))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: sandwich
#| check: true
target <- with(.envir_result, {
  u <- as.numeric(e)
  sqrt((bread %*% (t(X * u^2) %*% X) %*% bread)[2, 2])
})
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 2 && abs(.result[[2]] - target) < 1e-8) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("The robust standard error (%.3f) is noticeably larger than the classical one (%.3f). The classical formula was overconfident.", .result[[2]], .result[[1]]))
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The filling needs each observation's squared residual on the diagonal.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="sandwich"}
`diag(v)` puts the vector `v` on the diagonal of a matrix. You want the squared residuals there: `e^2`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="sandwich"}
```r
meat <- t(X) %*% diag(e^2) %*% X
V_robust <- bread %*% meat %*% bread
c(classical = summary(fit)$coefficients["x", "Std. Error"],
  robust    = sqrt(V_robust[2, 2]))
```

In real work you'd use `sandwich::vcovHC(fit, type = "HC0")` (or HC1–HC3, which make small-sample corrections), together with `lmtest::coeftest()`.
:::

### Does it matter? Check by simulation

A standard error is "right" if the 95% interval built from it covers the truth 95% of the time. Run this to compare the two methods over 1,000 simulated datasets. It takes a few seconds.

```{webr}
set.seed(10)
covers <- replicate(1000, {
  x <- runif(100, -3, 3)
  y <- 1 + 3 * x + x * rnorm(100)
  fit <- lm(y ~ x); X <- cbind(1, x); e <- residuals(fit)
  b <- coef(fit)[["x"]]
  se_classic <- summary(fit)$coefficients["x", "Std. Error"]
  bread <- solve(crossprod(X))
  se_robust <- sqrt((bread %*% crossprod(X * e) %*% bread)[2, 2])
  tq <- qt(0.975, 98)
  c(classic = abs(b - 3) < tq * se_classic, robust = abs(b - 3) < tq * se_robust)
})
rowMeans(covers)   # share of intervals that contain the true slope 3
```

::: {.column-margin}
[aim: 0.95]{.scribble}
:::

The classical intervals cover the truth noticeably less than 95% of the time: they claim more certainty than the data justify. The robust ones come close to 95%.

## Exercise 5: collinearity inflates variance

When two regressors move together, the regression struggles to separate their effects, and standard errors blow up. The lesson's formula is

$$
\text{var}(\hat\beta_j) = \sigma^2\,\frac{1}{1 - R_j^2}\,\frac{1}{\sum_i (x_{ij} - \bar x_j)^2},
$$

where $R_j^2$ comes from regressing $x_j$ on the other regressors. The factor $1/(1-R_j^2)$ is the **variance inflation factor** (VIF). Compute it for `x1`.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: vif
set.seed(5)
x2 <- rnorm(100)
x1 <- 0.95 * x2 + sqrt(1 - 0.95^2) * rnorm(100)   # correlation about 0.95
y  <- 1 + 2 * x1 + 2 * x2 + rnorm(100)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: vif
R2_1 <- summary(lm(x1 ~ x2))$r.squared
VIF  <- ______
VIF
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: vif
#| check: true
target <- with(.envir_result, 1 / (1 - summary(lm(x1 ~ x2))$r.squared))
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1 && abs(.result - target) < 1e-8) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = sprintf("VIF = %.1f: the variance of the x1 coefficient is about %.0f times what it would be with uncorrelated regressors, so its standard error is about %.1f times larger.", target, target, sqrt(target)))
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "VIF is 1 divided by (1 minus R²).")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="vif"}
`1 / (1 - R2_1)`
:::

::: {.solution exercise="vif"}
```r
R2_1 <- summary(lm(x1 ~ x2))$r.squared
VIF  <- 1 / (1 - R2_1)
VIF
```

A common rule of thumb flags VIFs above 10. Collinearity doesn't bias the estimates; it makes them imprecise. Often the honest conclusion is "the data can't separate these two effects".
:::

## Exercise 6: a t-test is a regression

Two groups, A and B. A classic two-sample t-test (with equal variances) asks whether their means differ. The lesson claimed a regression on a group dummy is *the same test*. Complete the t-test call so it assumes equal variances, and compare its t statistic with the regression's.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ttest
set.seed(8)
group <- factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 30))
y <- c(rnorm(30, 10, 2), rnorm(30, 11, 2))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ttest
reg <- summary(lm(y ~ group))$coefficients
tt  <- t.test(y ~ group, var.equal = ______)

c(regression_t = reg["groupB", "t value"], t_test_t = unname(tt$statistic))
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ttest
#| check: true
if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 2 && isTRUE(all.equal(abs(.result[[1]]), abs(.result[[2]])))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Same number (up to the sign, which just depends on which group is subtracted from which). A dummy-variable regression and the equal-variance t-test make identical assumptions.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "The two t statistics should match in size. Did you tell t.test() to assume equal variances?")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ttest"}
The argument takes a logical value: `TRUE` or `FALSE`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ttest"}
```r
reg <- summary(lm(y ~ group))$coefficients
tt  <- t.test(y ~ group, var.equal = TRUE)
c(regression_t = reg["groupB", "t value"], t_test_t = unname(tt$statistic))
```
:::

## Free play

A scratchpad with the wage data loaded. Some ideas: add an interaction `educ:exper`; compare `wage` with `log(wage)` as the outcome and interpret the coefficient each way; plot `residuals(fit)` against `fitted(fit)` and look for patterns.

```{webr}
set.seed(1)
n <- 50
educ  <- round(runif(n, 8, 20))
exper <- round(runif(n, 0, 30))
wage  <- exp(1 + 0.08 * educ + 0.02 * exper + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3))
d <- data.frame(wage, educ, exper)

fit <- lm(log(wage) ~ educ + exper, data = d)
plot(fitted(fit), residuals(fit), pch = 19, col = "#1B2559AA")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
```
